samf-senior-2023-r1-01.title: Smaller case
samf-senior-2023-r1-01.body:
Like $\frac{10^3}{10^2} = \frac{1000}{100} = 10$: dividing consecutive powers of 10 always gives 10.

**Answer: (A) 1**

samf-senior-2023-r1-02.title: Counterexamples
samf-senior-2023-r1-02.body:
(i) is false: 2 is an even prime. (ii) is false: $2^3 = 8$ is even. (iii) is true: $2, 4, 6, \ldots$ never ends. Only (iii).

**Answer: (D) only (iii)**

samf-senior-2023-r1-02.title: Eliminate
samf-senior-2023-r1-02.body:
Any option containing (i) or (ii) is wrong because of the counterexamples $2$ and $8$. That leaves (D).

**Answer: (D) only (iii)**

samf-senior-2023-r1-03.title: Add flight time and time difference
Durban time first
samf-senior-2023-r1-03.body:
Arrival in Durban time: $09{:}55 + 8{:}20 = 18{:}15$. Dubai is 2 hours ahead: $20{:}15$.

**Answer: (A) 20:15**

samf-senior-2023-r1-05.title: Diameter equals the height
samf-senior-2023-r1-05.body:
The large circle touches the top and bottom sides, so its diameter is 18 and its radius is 9. Area $= \pi\cdot 9^2 = 81\pi$.

**Answer: (B) $81\pi$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-05.title: Check consistency
samf-senior-2023-r1-05.body:
The small circle (radius $r$) touches the bottom, the right side and the large circle. With the large centre at $(9, 9)$ and the small at $(25 - r, r)$: $(16 - r)^2 + (9 - r)^2 = (9 + r)^2$ gives $r^2 - 68r + 256 = 0$, $r = 4$. So the figure is consistent, and the large circle has area $81\pi$.

**Answer: (B) $81\pi$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-06.title: Two phases
samf-senior-2023-r1-06.body:
In the first 3 minutes she types 180 words. Then her rate is $0.75\times 60 = 45$ words per minute, and the remaining 720 words take $720\div 45 = 16$ minutes. Total $3 + 16 = 19$.

**Answer: (A) 19**

samf-senior-2023-r1-09.title: Parity
samf-senior-2023-r1-09.body:
Debbie is off $0, 8, 16, 24, \ldots$ days from today — always an even number of days. Refilwe is off $1, 7, 13, 19, \ldots$ days from today — always odd. An even number never equals an odd number, so they are never off together.

**Answer: (E) Never**

samf-senior-2023-r1-09.title: Congruences
samf-senior-2023-r1-09.body:
We would need $n\equiv 0 \pmod 8$ and $n\equiv 1\pmod 6$. The first makes $n$ even, the second makes $n$ odd — impossible.

**Answer: (E) Never**

samf-senior-2023-r1-10.title: Prime factorization
samf-senior-2023-r1-10.body:
$2023 = 7\times 289 = 7\times 17^2$. A perfect square needs every prime to an even power, so we must multiply by 7 (giving $7^2\cdot 17^2 = 119^2$).

**Answer: (C) 7**

samf-senior-2023-r1-10.title: Check the options
samf-senior-2023-r1-10.body:
$2023$ is not a square ($44^2 = 1936$, $45^2 = 2025$). Any multiplier $k$ making $2023k$ a square must be a multiple of 7, since 7 divides 2023 exactly once. The smallest is $k = 7$: $2023\cdot 7 = 14161 = 119^2$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) 7**

samf-senior-2023-r1-11.title: Powers of 2
samf-senior-2023-r1-11.body:
Hippy ends with $20\cdot 2^{20}$. Happy has $80\cdot 2^x = 20\cdot 2^{x+2}$ after $x$ hours. Equal when $x + 2 = 20$, i.e. $x = 18$.

**Answer: (D) 18**

samf-senior-2023-r1-11.title: Head start
samf-senior-2023-r1-11.body:
R80 is R20 doubled twice, so Happy starts "2 hours ahead" of Hippy and needs only $20 - 2 = 18$ hours.

**Answer: (D) 18**

samf-senior-2023-r1-12.title: Counting bound
samf-senior-2023-r1-12.body:
Each edge lies on exactly 2 faces, so $k$ red edges touch at most $2k$ faces. Covering all 6 faces needs $2k\ge 6$, i.e. $k\ge 3$. And 3 suffice: choose three edges, one in each direction, no two on a common face (see the example in the second solution); together they touch all $3\times 2 = 6$ faces.

**Answer: (B) 3**

samf-senior-2023-r1-12.title: Explicit example
samf-senior-2023-r1-12.body:
Label the faces top, bottom, front, back, left, right. Colour red: the front-top edge (covers front and top), the back-left edge (covers back and left), the bottom-right edge (covers bottom and right). All six faces have a red edge with only 3 red edges, and 2 would cover at most 4 faces.

**Answer: (B) 3**

samf-senior-2023-r1-13.title: Isosceles triangle
samf-senior-2023-r1-13.body:
The pentagon's interior angle is $\frac{540^\circ}{5} = 108^\circ$, so around $B$: $\angle FBC = 360^\circ - 108^\circ - 90^\circ = 162^\circ$. Since $BF = AB = BC$, triangle $BFC$ is isosceles, so $\angle BFC = \frac{180^\circ - 162^\circ}{2} = 9^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) 9**

samf-senior-2023-r1-13.title: Exterior angle
samf-senior-2023-r1-13.body:
Extend $AB$ beyond $B$. The angle between this extension and $BC$ is the pentagon's exterior angle $72^\circ$, and the angle between the extension and $BF$ is $90^\circ$. So $\angle CBF = 72^\circ + 90^\circ = 162^\circ$ (measured through the outside), and the base angles of isosceles $\triangle BCF$ are $\frac{18^\circ}{2} = 9^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) 9**

samf-senior-2023-r1-14.title: Classify the routes
Count by complement
samf-senior-2023-r1-14.body:
Routes avoiding $X$ go along the bottom arc from $A$ directly to $Y$ (1 way) and then on to $B$ (3 ways): 3 routes. All routes: $11$ (count paths into each point: $X$ gets 2, $Y$ gets $2\cdot 1 + 1 = 3$, $B$ gets $2 + 3\cdot 3 = 11$). So $\frac{11 - 3}{11} = \frac8{11}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac8{11}$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-15.title: Difference of sectors
samf-senior-2023-r1-15.body:
The blade (42 cm) starts 18 cm from the pivot, so it sweeps the region between sectors of radius $60$ and $18$ with angle $160^\circ = \frac49$ of a full turn:
$$\frac49\pi(60^2 - 18^2) = \frac49\pi\cdot 3276 = 1456\pi.$$

**Answer: (D) $1456\pi$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-16.title: Vertical base
samf-senior-2023-r1-16.body:
The points $(a, b\pm c)$ lie on the vertical line $x = a$, a distance $2c$ apart: take this as the base. The third vertex $(-a, c)$ is at horizontal distance $2a$ from that line, the height. Area $= \frac12\cdot 2c\cdot 2a = 2ac$.

**Answer: (A) $2ac$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-16.title: Test numbers
samf-senior-2023-r1-16.body:
With $a = b = c = 1$: vertices $(1, 2), (1, 0), (-1, 1)$, base 2, height 2, area 2. Options: $2ac = 2$ ✓, $2bc = 2$, $b(a+c) = 2$, $c(a-b) = 0$, $2+2b+c = 5$. Try $a = 2, b = c = 1$: vertices $(2,2),(2,0),(-2,1)$, area $\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 4 = 4$; $2ac = 4$ ✓ but $2bc = 2$ and $b(a+c) = 3$. So $2ac$.

**Answer: (A) $2ac$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-17.title: Area two ways
samf-senior-2023-r1-17.body:
From the figure, $AF = 9$ is the height onto $CD$ and $CE = 11$ is the height onto $AD$. The area of the parallelogram is base × height in two ways: $CD\cdot AF = AD\cdot CE$, so $12\cdot 9 = 11\cdot AD$ and $AD = \frac{108}{11}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{108}{11}$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-17.title: Similar triangles
samf-senior-2023-r1-17.body:
Right triangles $ADF$ and $CDE$ share the angle at $D$, so they are similar: $\frac{AD}{CD} = \frac{AF}{CE} = \frac9{11}$. With $CD = AB = 12$: $AD = \frac{108}{11}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{108}{11}$**

samf-senior-2023-r1-18.title: Overlap of green windows
samf-senior-2023-r1-18.body:
Each light's cycle is shifted 10 s from the previous one, so the green phases are shifted too. If light 1 turns green at time $t$, light 8 turns green at $t + 70$. Light 1 stays green for 90 s, until $t + 90$. All eight are green from $t + 70$ to $t + 90$: 20 seconds. (Light 8's previous green ended long before, since a full cycle lasts 183 s.)

**Answer: (C) 20**

samf-senior-2023-r1-18.title: Intersection of intervals
samf-senior-2023-r1-18.body:
Green intervals: $[t, t + 90]$, $[t + 10, t + 100]$, …, $[t + 70, t + 160]$. Their intersection is $[t + 70, t + 90]$, of length $90 - 70 = 20$ s.

**Answer: (C) 20**

samf-senior-2023-r1-19.title: Count layers
samf-senior-2023-r1-19.body:
Let $x, y, z$ be the areas covered by exactly 1, 2, 3 layers. Floor covered: $x + y + z = 64$. Total rug area counts each region once per layer: $x + 2y + 3z = 150$. With $z = 28$: $x + y = 36$ and $x + 2y = 66$, so $y = 30$.

**Answer: (A) 30**

samf-senior-2023-r1-19.title: Subtract directly
samf-senior-2023-r1-19.body:
Subtract the two equations: $(x + 2y + 3z) - (x + y + z) = y + 2z = 150 - 64 = 86$. So $y = 86 - 56 = 30$.

**Answer: (A) 30**

samf-senior-2023-r1-20.title: Count each type of stroke
samf-senior-2023-r1-20.body:
Effects on (heads, tails): two heads $(-2, 0)$; one tail $(0, +1)$; two tails $(+1, -2)$; one head $(0, 0)$ is useless. Let $x, y, z$ be the numbers of two-head, one-tail, two-tail strokes. To go from $(3,3)$ to $(0,0)$:
$$3 - 2x + z = 0,\qquad 3 + y - 2z = 0.$$
So $z = 2x - 3$ and $y = 2z - 3 = 4x - 9$. Since $y\ge 0$, $x\ge 3$ (as $x$ is an integer), and then the total $x + y + z = 7x - 12$ is smallest for $x = 3$: $y = z = 3$, total $9$.

It can be done: repeat "one tail, two tails, two heads" three times: $(h, t)\to(h, t+1)\to(h+1, t-1)\to(h-1, t-1)$, taking $(3,3)\to(2,2)\to(1,1)\to(0,0)$.

**Answer: (D) 9**

samf-senior-2023-r1-20.title: Think backwards about tails
samf-senior-2023-r1-20.body:
Every tail must eventually disappear in a "two tails" stroke, and each such stroke adds a head. "One tail" adds a tail. If $y$ "one tail" strokes are used, $3 + y$ tails must be removed in pairs, so $z = \frac{3+y}{2}$ "two tails" strokes, adding $z$ heads; then $3 + z$ heads are removed in pairs by $x = \frac{3+z}{2}$ "two heads" strokes. $y$ must be odd, so $y\ge 1$ gives $z = 2$ and $x = 2.5$ — not an integer; $y = 3$ gives $z = 3$, $x = 3$, total 9. Larger $y$ only increases the total. (A computer search over all states confirms 9.)

**Answer: (D) 9**
